NBC News: Caleb Flynn, former 'American Idol' singer, found guilty of wife's murder

content.p: At about 2:30 on the morning of 16 February 2026, Caleb Flynn called 911 from his home in Tipp City, Ohio, north of Dayton. "Somebody broke into my home and shot my wife," he said. Police found Ashley Flynn, 37, dead in bed with two gunshot wounds to the head. Three days later they arrested her husband. On 29 September 2026 a Miami County jury found him guilty of aggravated murder and eight other counts, accepting the prosecution's case that he had shot her as she slept, staged a break-in, and done it to be with a woman from his church.

Flynn, a former music pastor who had auditioned for "American Idol" in 2013, pleaded not guilty and maintains that he is innocent. His lawyer has said he will appeal. He faces up to life in prison without parole.

Ashley Flynn graduated from Tippecanoe High School in 2006 and from Lee University in 2010, then went to work for Tipp City Schools. She was a classroom teacher, later a substitute teacher, and coached seventh-grade volleyball at Tippecanoe Middle School. She also taught at LifeWise Academy, a Christian nonprofit that gives Bible instruction to public school students. The couple had two daughters.

Her mother, Jill Smith, testified that the two of them were best friends. She said the marriage had seemed somewhat strained in its last six months, but that Ashley never spoke badly of her husband. "She always wanted us to think the best of Caleb," she said. Eight days after the shooting the family marked what would have been her 38th birthday.

Ashley had encouraged her husband's singing. In footage recorded for Season 12 of "American Idol" he said his wife had nudged him to audition and that he loved her more than anything. CBS News reported that he was given a ticket to the Hollywood round and was cut early. NBC News said he did not advance to the main competition.

Officers were sent at about 2:31 a.m. to a reported burglary in progress. Flynn and the couple's children were in the house. He told the dispatcher that the door leading to the garage was wide open and that he did not know whether the intruder was still inside. Police set up a perimeter and searched with dogs and a drone. They found nobody. The first public statements described an apparent burglary with signs of forced entry.

Flynn's own account varied. On police body-camera footage he said he had gone to lie down in his daughters' room and heard the shot from there. In recorded interviews played in court he said he had been asleep on the couch. He told an investigator that day that he and his wife had no marital problems at all. He also said that a man had come to the house the day before, handed his wife an American flag and made a strange sales pitch.

When police arrived, the garage door, a side door and the centre console of Flynn's pickup truck were open. He told them he kept a gun in the console. It was not there, and the weapon used in the killing has never been found.

The FBI and the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation joined Tipp City police. On 19 February Flynn, then 39, was arrested and booked into the Miami County Jail. Court documents alleged that he shot his wife with a 9mm handgun and staged the scene. Police chief Gregory Adkins called the investigation complex and gave no details. At his arraignment the next morning Flynn pleaded not guilty, and bond was set at $2 million. His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, complained of a "seeming rush to judgment".

The centre of the trial, which opened on 18 September, was the testimony of Alleigha Botner, 24. By her account she was a 20-year-old intern at his church when they met, and the affair was still going on when Ashley died. CBS News put its length at roughly 18 months, and CNN at nearly two years. Over two days she read from their messages, which prosecutors numbered at more than 100,000.

Many expressed hatred of his wife. "I just want her dead and gone," he wrote in early 2025. On 11 February 2025, almost exactly a year before the shooting, he wrote: "I need her to die, to cheat again, to leave." On 24 March 2025 Botner asked, "What can I do?" and he answered, "Kill her." In August 2025, according to NBC News, he wrote that he had been up until 4 a.m. "trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail".

Botner said she set him a series of deadlines to leave the marriage, the last on 11 January 2026, and then cut off contact until 14 February. The night before the killing he wrote, "Actions will come tomorrow," and, "I choose you. I'm free." She told the court she took "actions" to mean a divorce. When a church member told her the next morning that Ashley was dead, she said, "It seemed like too much of a coincidence that the day he's divorcing her, she's just dead all of a sudden." Hours later, at the home of Ashley's parents, Flynn hugged her and, by her account, said: "It didn't happen the way we thought it would, did it?"

Botner admitted that she had lied to the FBI at first, and that she had told Flynn in one message that she wanted to kill his wife, which she said she regretted. She was not charged and said she had been offered nothing for her testimony. Her phone and laptop were lost weeks before the shooting, one in water on a trip to Florida and the other on a flight. The defence suggested that was no coincidence. Ring camera video showed she was at home when the murder took place.

FBI Special Agent Sarah Deamron testified that the garage side door bore no pry, kick or ram marks on the outside. The gouge marks were on the inside trim of the frame. She said she had seen about 75 doors forced open and that this one did not match a forced entry.

A digital forensics examiner said Flynn's devices recorded roughly 200 steps at intervals in the hour before the 911 call, and another 346 around the time of the call. "The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving," assistant prosecutor Matthew C. Joseph told the jury. Prosecuting attorney Paul Watkins said Flynn had taken down the home's security cameras twenty days before the killing, including one that covered the way in from the garage, and that on the day of the shooting he deleted apps and tried to delete messages. Another FBI agent, Andrea Kinzig, said she found nothing on Ashley's phone to support Flynn's claim to Botner that his wife was having an affair.

Joseph argued that playing the victim let Flynn keep what a divorce would have cost him: a well-paid job in his wife's family business, her life insurance, his daughters and his standing as a worship leader.

Flynn's lawyers conceded the affair. "A man can fail as a husband without being a murderer," Emily Smith said in her opening statement. Mulligan called the case circumstantial. He pointed out that Flynn had spoken to detectives three times voluntarily, agreed to searches of his home and phone and given his fingerprints. "Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case," he said. The defence called no witnesses, and Flynn did not take the stand. Mulligan said afterwards that the jury had already heard his client's account three times in the police interviews.

The jury returned on the afternoon of Tuesday 29 September after between two and two and a half hours, by the various accounts. It found Flynn guilty of aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two of felonious assault and three of tampering with evidence, and found that he used a firearm in seven of them. Flynn wept as Judge Jeannine Pratt read the verdicts. She revoked his bond and set sentencing for 5 October.

"People lie. Evidence doesn't," Watkins had said in closing. Outside court he read a statement from Ashley's family, who said that "no verdict can bring Ashley back". He asked people to turn their attention from the defendant to her. "This world would be a much better place if all of us in it lived like Ashley," he said.

Mulligan said he expected an appeal and named one ground: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design." He said the sentence for aggravated murder in Ohio ranges from 20 years to life up to life without parole.
